chapters.name: Regulation of Securities and Issuers
chapters.spine: Nothing in the Act switches on until the thing being sold is a security. Answer that question, then ask whether registration is required, then ask by which method. Three filters, always in that order. Only five questions come from this chapter, but the definitions you build here are quoted back at you in all seven of the others.

cells.title: Definition of a security, and the Howey test
refs: Achievable Ch. 1 Definitions — Issuers & securities (Howey test)
STC 43e Ch. 1 Key Terms — Security, p. 6; Ch. 2 Securities, p. 16

items.x: The Act defines “security” with a long list of named instruments — stock, treasury stock, bonds, debentures, notes, evidences of indebtedness, collateral trust certificates, transferable shares, voting trust certificates, preorganization subscriptions, certificates of interest in oil, gas or mining titles, warrants and rights to subscribe — and then closes with a catch-all for anything commonly known as a security. The list is deliberately open-ended. That design choice is the whole point: substance governs, not the label on the paperwork.

Because the list cannot anticipate every arrangement, the catch-all carries the term “investment contract,” and the Supreme Court supplied the four-part test for what an investment contract is. All four prongs must be present: an investment of money, in a common enterprise, with an expectation of profits, derived primarily from the efforts of others.
The four Howey prongs, in order: money in · common enterprise · expectation of profit · profits from the efforts of others.

The fourth prong is where most novel arrangements are decided. If the investor does the work — a person who buys a franchise and runs it themselves — there is no security. If a promoter does the work and the investor waits for a check, there usually is one. Orange groves paired with a cultivation contract, working interests in an oil well managed by the operator, fractional interests in racehorses managed by a trainer, and tokens sold with a promise that the issuing team will build the network all come out the same way.
“It is real estate, so it cannot be a security.” Wrong. Real estate sold with a management contract that produces passive income for the buyer is the original Howey fact pattern.
Feeds SEC-2 (what is excluded), SEC-4 and SEC-5 (exemptions apply only once something IS a security), and REM-2 (the Administrator’s jurisdiction attaches to offers and sales of securities).

cells.title: What is not a security
refs: Achievable Ch. 1 Definitions — Securities (what is excluded)

items.x: A short list of product families sits outside the definition, and the organizing idea is who bears the investment risk. If the issuer or insurer guarantees the outcome and absorbs the market risk, it is not a security. If the buyer absorbs the market risk, it is.

Not securities: fixed annuities and fixed insurance products · whole life and endowment policies · commodity futures contracts · physical commodities and precious metals held directly · collectibles, art, rare coins · bank certificates of deposit, savings accounts, demand deposits · real estate owned directly for personal use or investment without a management arrangement · retirement plan interests such as IRAs and 401(k) accounts themselves (the investments inside them are another matter).

Variable products are securities. In a variable annuity or variable life contract the contract holder’s account value moves with a separate account portfolio, so the holder bears the investment risk. You know this cold from the hedging side of your work: a fixed annuity leaves the insurer holding the market exposure, which is why the carrier hedges it on its own balance sheet; a variable contract passes that exposure through to the policyholder, which is why the separate account is registered.
Selling a variable product requires a securities registration (Series 6 or 7 plus the state exam) AND a state insurance license. Selling a fixed annuity requires only the insurance license.

Equity-indexed and index-linked annuities are the genuinely contested middle. Where the contract guarantees principal and credits a formula-driven return, most states treat it as insurance; where the buyer takes real downside, it looks like a security. The exam avoids the hard cases — if a question says “fixed” it means not a security, and if it says “variable” it means security.

“A fixed annuity is a security because the return depends on an investment portfolio.” Wrong — the insurer guarantees the rate and holds the risk. This is described as the single most recycled distinction in this chapter, and it is worth being able to answer without pausing.

“A bank CD is never a security.” Mostly true and it is the exam answer — but know the edge: a long-dated brokered CD with unusual features that trades in a secondary market can be recharacterized. If the stem says “certificate of deposit at an insured bank,” answer not a security.

cells.title: Offer, sale, and the events that are neither
refs: STC 43e Ch. 7 Offers and Sales, p. 135; Gifts of Securities, p. 139

items.x: The Act does not regulate securities in the abstract; it regulates offers and sales of them. A sale is any contract of sale, contract to sell, or disposition of a security for value. An offer is any attempt to dispose of a security, or any solicitation of an offer to buy, for value. The operative phrase in both is “for value.” No value moving, no sale.
Note how far “offer” reaches: an attempt counts. The pitch that fails is still an offer, and it is still within the Administrator’s jurisdiction and still subject to the antifraud rules.

These ARE sales even though they look like gifts or non-events: a gift of ASSESSABLE stock (the recipient takes on a future obligation, which is value) · any security given as a bonus with the purchase of anything else, security or not · a warrant or right delivered together with a bond.
The sale of a warrant, right, or convertible security is also an OFFER of the underlying security it can be converted into or used to buy.

These are NOT sales: a bona fide gift of non-assessable stock · a bona fide pledge or loan of securities as collateral · a stock dividend or stock split where the holder gives nothing · a merger, consolidation, reclassification, or sale of assets approved by a vote of the security holders · an exchange of securities in a judicially approved reorganization.

Keep “not a sale” and “exempt transaction” in separate drawers. An exempt transaction IS a sale that happens to skip registration. An excluded event is not a sale at all, so no registration analysis ever begins.
“The stock was free, so no sale occurred.” Wrong when the free security rides along with a purchase — part of the price is attributed to it, and both instruments were sold.

cells.title: Exempt securities — exempt because of what they are

items.x: An exempt security is exempt from REGISTRATION because of the nature of the instrument or its issuer. The status attaches to the security and travels with it into every subsequent transaction, forever. Once exempt, always exempt.

The list: U.S. government and agency securities · Canadian federal and provincial government securities · securities of foreign governments with which the U.S. maintains diplomatic relations · municipal securities of any state or political subdivision · securities issued by banks, savings institutions, and trust companies · securities issued by insurance companies · securities of federally regulated public utilities and common carriers · securities of nonprofit religious, educational, charitable, fraternal, and social organizations · commercial paper · securities issued in connection with employee benefit plans · securities of federal covered status.

Commercial paper qualifies only if all three conditions hold: maturity of nine months or less, denominations of at least $50,000, and a rating in one of the three highest categories from a nationally recognized rating organization.
Bank securities means the BANK. A bank HOLDING COMPANY’s stock is not exempt. Any time a stem inserts the words “holding company,” the exemption is gone.

Insurance company securities are exempt — meaning the insurer’s own stock and bonds. The variable annuity and variable life contracts the insurer sells are separate-account securities and are NOT covered by that exemption. Two different things issued by the same company, two different answers.

Notice what unites the list: issuers already supervised by another regulator, or governments. The theory is that a second layer of state merit review adds nothing. That is also why the exemption never touches fraud — see SEC-6.

cells.title: Exempt transactions — exempt because of how the sale happens

items.x: A transaction exemption looks at the circumstances of a particular trade rather than at the instrument. It is single-use. It covers the transaction described and nothing after it; the next trade in the same security has to find its own exemption or register.

The heavily tested ones: an isolated non-issuer transaction · any transaction with an institutional investor · a private placement directed to no more than ten non-institutional persons in the state in twelve consecutive months · a preorganization certificate offered to no more than ten subscribers · an unsolicited order received from a customer · a transaction by a fiduciary — executor, administrator, receiver, trustee in bankruptcy, sheriff, marshal, conservator, guardian · a non-issuer transaction in a security listed in a recognized securities manual · an offer or sale to existing security holders where no commission is paid.

The private placement exemption carries two conditions beyond the count: the seller must reasonably believe every non-institutional buyer is purchasing for investment rather than resale, and no commission or other remuneration may be paid for soliciting a non-institutional buyer.
The preorganization exemption carries its own two: no payment may be received from any subscriber, and no commission may be paid for soliciting them.

Institutional investors are counted separately and without limit. The ten-person cap governs only non-institutional persons. Ten retail persons plus fifty institutions is fine. Your world lives almost entirely inside this exemption — an offering placed with insurance carriers and pension funds does not touch the ten-person cap at all.
“The eleventh institution defeats the private placement exemption.” Wrong — institutions do not count.

“Because the first sale was exempt, later sales of the same security are exempt.” Wrong — that is the exempt-SECURITY rule, not the exempt-TRANSACTION rule. This swap is the most common way this chapter is tested.

Compare with federal law once and move on: the state private placement exemption counts ten or fewer non-institutional persons; the federal Regulation D Rule 506 exemption counts thirty-five or fewer non-accredited investors. Because Rule 506 securities became federal covered, the state exemption is now largely vestigial in practice — but it is still fully testable.

cells.title: Federal covered securities, notice filing, and the antifraud floor
refs: Achievable 2.5 Securities; Ch. 1 Definitions — Exempt & excluded
STC 43e Ch. 2 Federal Exemptions, p. 35; Anti-Fraud Provisions, p. 37

items.x: In 1996 Congress redrew the federal-state line. For certain categories, states are preempted from requiring registration at all. Those are federal covered securities. What states retain is narrow and specific: a notice filing with a fee, and full antifraud authority.

Four categories of federal covered security: securities listed on a national exchange (and any security of equal or senior rank to a listed one) · securities issued by registered investment companies · securities sold to qualified purchasers · securities sold under Regulation D Rule 506.

Only two of the four are actually required to notice file: investment company securities, and Rule 506 offerings. Issuers of exchange-listed securities and of securities sold to qualified purchasers do not notice file.

A notice filing consists of: a statement identifying the issuer and the security, copies of what was filed with the SEC (or where to get them), a consent to service of process, and the state fee. For mutual funds it is typically renewed annually.

What the state can still do with a federal covered security: refuse a deficient or unpaid filing, investigate and prosecute fraud, and suspend transactions where fraud is found. What it cannot do: review the merits, require registration by coordination or qualification, or impose disclosure obligations beyond the federal ones.
Rule 506 is federal covered. Rule 504 is not. (Rule 505 was repealed in 2016 and should not appear — if it does, it is a distractor.)

The one rule with no exceptions anywhere in this subject: nothing is ever exempt from the antifraud provisions. Not an exempt security, not an exempt transaction, not a federal covered security, not any person. Exemption relieves the duty to register. It never relieves the duty to deal honestly. When a stem asks which of four items is exempt from the antifraud provisions, the answer is none of them.

cells.title: The three registration methods
refs: STC 43e Ch. 2 Types of State Securities Registration, p. 23

items.x: A security that is neither federal covered nor exempt must register in every state where it is offered. There are three doors, and which one an issuer uses is determined by its federal status, not by preference.
Registration by FILING (also called notification) — the streamlined path for seasoned issuers with an established earnings history. Rarely used today.
Registration by COORDINATION — for a security registering with the SEC at the same time under the Securities Act of 1933. This is the common path for a public offering.

Registration by QUALIFICATION — the fallback for everything else, including intrastate offerings that never go to the SEC. The most demanding: full disclosure of the issuer, its capital structure, its officers and directors, the use of proceeds, audited financials, and an opinion of counsel that the security is legally issued, fully paid and non-assessable.

Coordination becomes effective automatically and simultaneously with the federal registration, provided no stop order is in effect, the registration statement has been on file with the ADMINISTRATOR for the required period, and a statement of the maximum and minimum proposed offering prices and maximum underwriting discounts has been on file with the Administrator for two full business days.
Qualification becomes effective only when the Administrator affirmatively declares it effective. There is no automatic mechanism.

Every method requires, in addition to the substantive filing: a consent to service of process, the filing fee, and whatever information about the issuer, the offering, and the underwriters the Administrator requires. The Administrator may also require an escrow or an impound of proceeds, and may require sales to be made through a specified escrow agent.
The ten-day clock in coordination runs with the state Administrator, not the SEC. A stem that says “on file with the SEC for ten days” is describing the wrong filing.
“Qualification becomes effective automatically after thirty days.” Wrong — that is the PERSON registration clock (see BDR-5). Securities registered by qualification wait for the Administrator to act.

cells.title: Life of a securities registration, and stop orders
refs: STC 43e Ch. 2 Registering Securities, pp. 21–22; Denial, Suspension, Revocation, p. 26

items.x: A securities registration is effective for one year from its effective date. This is the only registration under the Act that does not expire on December 31 — persons all expire at calendar year end. Expect that contrast to be tested.
The registration statement may be filed by the issuer, by any other person on whose behalf the offering is being made, or by a registered broker-dealer.
The Administrator’s kill switch is the stop order, which denies, suspends, or revokes the effectiveness of a registration statement. It requires grounds, and the grounds are enumerated.

Grounds for a stop order include: the registration statement is incomplete or contains a material misstatement or omission · the offering violates the Act or an order · the issuer’s enterprise or method of business is illegal · the offering would work a fraud on purchasers · underwriter compensation or promoters’ profits are unreasonable · the applicable filing fee was not paid · the security is the subject of an injunction by a court.

Due process: a stop order may not be entered without prior written notice to the applicant and every person on record, an opportunity for a hearing, and written findings of fact and conclusions of law. The Administrator MAY summarily postpone or suspend effectiveness pending final determination, but must then promptly notify the parties and hold a hearing on request — within fifteen days of a written request.

The Administrator may not enter a stop order based on facts known when the registration became effective unless the proceeding is instituted within thirty days after effectiveness. The Act does not let a regulator sit on knowledge and then pull the rug.
A stop order may be modified or vacated by the Administrator at any time if conditions change.

chapters.name: Regulation of Broker-Dealers
chapters.spine: Two questions decide every broker-dealer fact pattern: does the firm have a place of business in this state, and who are its in-state customers? Everything else in this chapter — forms, fees, bonds, clocks — is what happens after you answer yes. Note what is NOT here: the federal net capital dollar ladder. This is a state law exam and the state’s authority over a firm’s finances is capped at whatever the SEC already requires.

cells.title: Definition of a broker-dealer
refs: STC 43e Ch. 1 Person, p. 7; Ch. 3 State Registration of Broker-Dealers, p. 43

items.x: A broker-dealer is any PERSON engaged in the BUSINESS of effecting transactions in securities for the account of others or for its own account. Federal law splits broker and dealer into two definitions; state law fuses them into one. On this exam there is a single concept and a single registration.

Each element does work. “Person” includes entities and individuals. “Engaged in the business” requires a pattern, not a single trade — someone who sells a block of stock once is not a broker-dealer. “Effecting transactions” covers the whole arc from solicitation through settlement, not just execution.

Person under the Act means an individual, corporation, partnership, association, joint-stock company, trust where the beneficial interests are evidenced by a security, unincorporated organization, government, or political subdivision. It does NOT include a minor, a deceased individual, or a person judged mentally incompetent.
Most broker-dealers are firms, but a natural person operating a securities business as a sole proprietor is a broker-dealer, not an agent. The test is the role, not whether the actor breathes.
“Only an entity can be a broker-dealer.” Wrong — a sole proprietor qualifies.
→ AGT-1. An individual who REPRESENTS a broker-dealer is an agent. An individual who IS the broker-dealer is a broker-dealer.

cells.title: Exclusions from the definition
refs: Achievable 2.1 Broker-dealers — institution rule, vacation rule
STC 43e Ch. 3 Exclusions from the BD Definition, p. 45

items.x: Three categorical exclusions: agents · issuers · banks, savings institutions, and trust companies.

Then the conditional exclusion, which is where the exam lives. A firm with NO place of business in the state is excluded if its business in that state is limited to a permitted set of counterparties. This is sometimes called the institution rule.

The permitted counterparties: issuers of the securities involved in the transactions · other broker-dealers · banks, savings institutions, and trust companies · insurance companies · investment companies · pension or profit-sharing trusts · other financial institutions or institutional buyers, whether acting for themselves or as trustees.

Separately, the snowbird or vacation rule: a firm with no place of business in the state may continue to transact with an EXISTING customer who is temporarily present in that state and is not a resident of it.

Read the snowbird rule for what it actually protects — a relationship already in motion. It does not permit soliciting new customers in the temporary state, and it does not permit advertising into it. The relationship must predate the travel.
There is NO de minimis exemption for broker-dealers. A single in-state retail customer who resides in the state requires registration, no matter how institutional the rest of the book is.
The exclusion is conjunctive. No place of business AND only permitted counterparties. Satisfy one and fail the other and you register.

Your desk sits comfortably inside this exclusion in most states — an index solutions group dealing exclusively with insurance carriers and other institutions has no in-state retail customers. That intuition is correct and it is exactly what the rule is for. What breaks it is an office, not a client.

cells.title: Place of business and jurisdictional triggers
refs: STC 43e Ch. 3 Exclusions from the BD Definition, pp. 45–46

items.x: Registration is jurisdictional and the trigger is a disjunction: a place of business in the state, OR transacting business with residents of the state outside a permitted category. Either one is sufficient on its own.

A place of business is any office, branch, or location at which the firm regularly conducts business, and any address the firm publicly holds out as a business address — on a website, a business card, letterhead, or an advertisement.

Holding out matters as much as physical presence. A firm that lists a suite number in a state on its website has a place of business there even if nobody sits in it. Conversely, a hotel room used once, or an itinerant location where no clients are met and nothing is held out, is not one.
“The firm has no employees in the state, so it has no place of business.” Not necessarily — an address held out publicly is enough.

cells.title: The registration application
refs: STC 43e Ch. 3 The Application Process, p. 40

items.x: Four things go with every application: the application form itself (Form BD, filed electronically through the Central Registration Depository), a consent to service of process, the filing fee, and any surety bond the Administrator requires.

The consent to service of process is the item candidates skip and the exam does not. It irrevocably appoints the Administrator as the registrant’s attorney to receive service of legal papers, so an investor suing an out-of-state firm can serve the state regulator instead of chasing the firm. Three attributes get tested: it is irrevocable, it is filed once with the initial application, and — unlike the rest of the registration — it is never renewed.
Everyone files one: broker-dealers, agents, investment advisers, IARs, and issuers registering securities, including issuers of federal covered securities making a notice filing.
Filing fees are paid at initial registration and again annually at renewal. If an application is denied or withdrawn, the Administrator may retain all or part of the fee. It is not refunded.
When two registered firms merge or one acquires the other, the surviving successor firm must file an updated application — but pays no additional filing fee.

The Administrator may also require an applicant to pass a written or oral examination as a condition of registration, and may require the firm to publish an announcement of the application in a newspaper.

cells.title: Effectiveness, expiration, renewal, and withdrawal
refs: STC 43e Ch. 3 Effective Date and Expiration, p. 42; Ch. 7 Cancellations and Withdrawals, p. 145

items.x: A registration becomes effective at NOON on the THIRTIETH day after the application, or the last amendment to it, is filed.

Notice the direction of the default. The registration is granted unless the Administrator acts. The Administrator may accelerate it — which is routine in practice — but if the regulator does nothing, the applicant is registered. The burden of acting sits on the state.
The Administrator will not grant registration if a denial order is in effect, or if a proceeding for denial, revocation, suspension, cancellation, or withdrawal is pending.
Registrations of broker-dealers, agents, investment advisers, and IARs expire on December 31 each year regardless of when they became effective. Renewal is an updated application and a new fee.

Withdrawal becomes effective thirty days after the Administrator receives the application to withdraw, or sooner if the Administrator allows — unless a revocation or suspension proceeding is pending, in which case the Administrator controls the timing.

After withdrawal, the Administrator retains jurisdiction over the former registrant for ONE YEAR and may institute a revocation or suspension proceeding within that year for conduct that occurred while the person was registered.
“A firm can escape a pending investigation by withdrawing.” Wrong on two counts: withdrawal is suspended while a proceeding is pending, and jurisdiction survives for a year regardless.

cells.title: Net capital and surety bonds
refs: Achievable 2.1 Broker-dealers — net capital & NSMIA ceiling
STC 43e Ch. 3 Net Capital, p. 43; The Application Process (surety bond), pp. 41–42

items.x: The state’s power over a broker-dealer’s balance sheet exists, but it is capped. The Administrator may require a minimum net capital in the public interest, and may require a surety bond — but may not impose a requirement exceeding what the SEC already requires. The same ceiling applies to bonding and to books-and-records rules. Federal law occupies the field above that line.
If a broker-dealer’s net capital falls below the required minimum, it must notify the Administrator of the state where its principal office is located within ONE business day.

The bond exists to make an investor’s judgment collectible. Its trigger is custody or discretionary authority over client assets — the two conditions under which a firm can actually lose someone’s money through misconduct rather than through markets.
Because broker-dealers almost always hold customer assets, they almost always need a bond. An investment adviser that takes neither custody nor discretion may need none.
No bond is required if the firm’s net capital, or an adviser’s minimum net worth, already meets the required minimum. Meeting the financial requirement substitutes for the bond.
The Administrator may accept a deposit of cash or securities in lieu of a bond — never personal property. Where securities are deposited, the Administrator determines which are acceptable.

A required bond must be maintained for as long as the registrant is in business and for three years afterward. Any bond must permit suit by a person with a cause of action under the civil liability section, and no suit may be brought on the bond more than two years after the sale or other act it is based on.

The bond must survive the bonded person. A cause of action under the Act survives the death of either party, so a bond that terminated on death or deregistration would defeat the statute. The Act does not permit one.

cells.title: Post-registration conduct: records, advertising, supervision
refs: STC 43e Ch. 3 Advertising and Sales Literature, p. 43; Maintenance Requirements, p. 44; Special Examination, p. 45

items.x: A registered broker-dealer must make and keep the records the Administrator requires, and all records are subject to reasonable periodic, special, or other examinations by the Administrator — inside or outside the state — as the Administrator deems necessary in the public interest.

Advertising, sales literature, prospectuses, pamphlets, circulars, and form letters relating to registered securities and distributed to current or prospective clients must be FILED with the Administrator. Advertising means any notice, circular, letter, or other written communication addressed to more than one person. A firm’s public website counts, because any investor can see it.
Even material that need not be filed still has to be fair, balanced, and not misleading. Filing is a procedural obligation layered on top of the substantive one, not a substitute for it.
Customer SECURITIES must be segregated from the firm’s own securities. Customer CASH may be commingled. The asymmetry is the tested part.

On the federal side, a firm must establish and maintain a supervisory system reasonably designed to achieve compliance: written supervisory procedures, registered principals designated for each line of business, review of correspondence and transactions, an annual compliance meeting with each registered person, and periodic inspection of offices. The state exam wants the existence and shape of that system, not the inspection calendar.
“The state may require a broker-dealer to keep records the SEC does not require.” Wrong — preempted.

cells.title: Canadian broker-dealers and other special cases
refs: Achievable 2.1 Broker-dealers — limited registration of Canadian broker-dealers
STC 43e Ch. 3 Rules for Canadian Broker-Dealers and Agents, p. 54

items.x: Canadian regulators helped draft the model act, which is why it contains a bespoke, lighter registration path for Canadian firms. The point of it is narrow: to let a Canadian firm keep serving a client who has moved to or is visiting the United States, and to service Canadian retirement accounts held by U.S. residents.

A Canadian broker-dealer with no office in the state may obtain a limited registration by filing: an application, a consent to service of process, evidence of its registration with the securities regulator in its home province, and evidence that it is a member in good standing of a self-regulatory organization or stock exchange in Canada.

Agents of such firms may obtain a parallel limited registration on the same basis. Both the firm and the agent must remain in good standing at home; losing that status ends the U.S. limited registration.

The permitted business is correspondingly narrow: transactions with or for an existing client of the firm who is temporarily present in the United States, and self-directed tax-advantaged Canadian retirement accounts of persons now residing in the state.

It does NOT include a minor, a deceased individual, or a person judged mentally incompetent.
Three categorical exclusions: agents · issuers · banks, savings institutions, and trust companies.

The permitted counterparties: issuers of the securities involved in the transactions · other broker-dealers · banks, savings institutions, and trust companies · insurance companies · investment companies · pension or profit-sharing trusts · other financial institutions or institutional buyers, whether acting for themselves or as trustees.

Separately, the snowbird or vacation rule: a firm with no place of business in the state may continue to transact with an EXISTING customer who is temporarily present in that state and is not a resident of it.
There is NO de minimis exemption for broker-dealers. A single in-state retail customer who resides in the state requires registration, no matter how institutional the rest of the book is.

A place of business is any office, branch, or location at which the firm regularly conducts business, and any address the firm publicly holds out as a business address — on a website, a business card, letterhead, or an advertisement.

Four things go with every application: the application form itself (Form BD, filed electronically through the Central Registration Depository), a consent to service of process, the filing fee, and any surety bond the Administrator requires.
Everyone files one: broker-dealers, agents, investment advisers, IARs, and issuers registering securities, including issuers of federal covered securities making a notice filing.
Filing fees are paid at initial registration and again annually at renewal. If an application is denied or withdrawn, the Administrator may retain all or part of the fee. It is not refunded.
When two registered firms merge or one acquires the other, the surviving successor firm must file an updated application — but pays no additional filing fee.
A registration becomes effective at NOON on the THIRTIETH day after the application, or the last amendment to it, is filed.
The Administrator will not grant registration if a denial order is in effect, or if a proceeding for denial, revocation, suspension, cancellation, or withdrawal is pending.
Registrations of broker-dealers, agents, investment advisers, and IARs expire on December 31 each year regardless of when they became effective. Renewal is an updated application and a new fee.

Withdrawal becomes effective thirty days after the Administrator receives the application to withdraw, or sooner if the Administrator allows — unless a revocation or suspension proceeding is pending, in which case the Administrator controls the timing.

After withdrawal, the Administrator retains jurisdiction over the former registrant for ONE YEAR and may institute a revocation or suspension proceeding within that year for conduct that occurred while the person was registered.
If a broker-dealer’s net capital falls below the required minimum, it must notify the Administrator of the state where its principal office is located within ONE business day.
Because broker-dealers almost always hold customer assets, they almost always need a bond. An investment adviser that takes neither custody nor discretion may need none.
No bond is required if the firm’s net capital, or an adviser’s minimum net worth, already meets the required minimum. Meeting the financial requirement substitutes for the bond.
The Administrator may accept a deposit of cash or securities in lieu of a bond — never personal property. Where securities are deposited, the Administrator determines which are acceptable.

A required bond must be maintained for as long as the registrant is in business and for three years afterward. Any bond must permit suit by a person with a cause of action under the civil liability section, and no suit may be brought on the bond more than two years after the sale or other act it is based on.

A registered broker-dealer must make and keep the records the Administrator requires, and all records are subject to reasonable periodic, special, or other examinations by the Administrator — inside or outside the state — as the Administrator deems necessary in the public interest.

Advertising, sales literature, prospectuses, pamphlets, circulars, and form letters relating to registered securities and distributed to current or prospective clients must be FILED with the Administrator. Advertising means any notice, circular, letter, or other written communication addressed to more than one person. A firm’s public website counts, because any investor can see it.
Customer SECURITIES must be segregated from the firm’s own securities. Customer CASH may be commingled. The asymmetry is the tested part.

A Canadian broker-dealer with no office in the state may obtain a limited registration by filing: an application, a consent to service of process, evidence of its registration with the securities regulator in its home province, and evidence that it is a member in good standing of a self-regulatory organization or stock exchange in Canada.

Agents of such firms may obtain a parallel limited registration on the same basis. Both the firm and the agent must remain in good standing at home; losing that status ends the U.S. limited registration.

chapters.name: Regulation of Broker-Dealer Agents
chapters.spine: One sentence carries this chapter: activity defines registration, never title. The exam will describe what a person does, withhold whether it matters, and ask whether they must register. Read the verbs. Then ask two follow-ups — whom do they represent, and where do they have an office or clients?

cells.title: Definition of an agent
refs: STC 43e Ch. 3 State Registration of Agents, p. 47

items.x: An agent is any INDIVIDUAL, other than a broker-dealer itself, who represents a broker-dealer or an issuer in effecting or attempting to effect purchases or sales of securities.

Three elements, each with a trap attached. Individual — only a natural person can be an agent; a firm never is. Representing a broker-dealer or issuer — the person is acting as the face of an entity. Effecting OR ATTEMPTING to effect — the definition reaches the whole sales process, so soliciting is agent activity even when nothing is ever bought.

Activities that require agent registration: soliciting purchases or sales by any means · taking or receiving customer orders, even if someone else enters them · executing trades · quoting prices to customers on the firm’s behalf · supervising any of the above.
“She never closed a sale, so she was not acting as an agent.” Wrong — attempting counts.

cells.title: Who is not an agent
refs: STC 43e Ch. 3 Agents of Broker-Dealers, p. 49; Managers as Agents, p. 52

items.x: The exclusion is functional. Employees whose duties are purely clerical or ministerial — receptionists, file clerks, cashiers, back-office and IT staff — are not agents, because they neither solicit nor effect transactions.

The exclusion ends at the first customer order. The moment a clerical employee takes an order, solicits a prospect, or makes a recommendation, registration is required regardless of job title, script, or supervision.

Officers, partners, and directors of a broker-dealer or an issuer who do not actually engage in securities transactions are not agents by virtue of their position — though see AGT-5, where some of them get registered automatically anyway.

“The firm calls her a compliance analyst, so she is not an agent.” The title is irrelevant in both directions. A person with an impressive title who never touches a transaction may not need registration; a person with no title who routinely takes orders does.

cells.title: Agents of issuers — the exclusions
refs: $2 Textbook Mod 2, Lesson 5 · p. 22; Lesson 7 · p. 29
STC 43e Ch. 3 Agents of Issuers, p. 48

items.x: This is the chapter’s hardest boundary and its most tested. An individual representing an ISSUER may be excluded from agent registration in specific situations. An individual representing a BROKER-DEALER never is — there are no parallel exclusions on that side.

An individual representing an issuer need not register when the transaction involves: an exempt security — government, municipal, bank, insurance company, public utility, railroad, nonprofit, commercial paper, employee benefit plan interests; or an exempt transaction; or a security covered by certain federal covered transactions.

A separate exclusion covers sales by an issuer’s representative to the issuer’s own existing employees, partners, or directors — but ONLY where no commission or other remuneration is paid for soliciting the sale.

The no-commission condition attaches to that one clause. It is not a general rule that any uncompensated issuer representative is excluded. A person selling the issuer’s stock to the general public without a commission still needs to register.

The structure here is a deliberate echo of the securities exemptions in SEC-4 and SEC-5. The Act reuses its own architecture: if the security or the transaction was safe enough to skip registration, the person selling it on the issuer’s behalf is treated the same way.
→ SEC-4, SEC-5. If you cannot recall the exempt-security list, you cannot answer this cell.

cells.title: Where an agent must register
refs: STC 43e Ch. 3 Agent Exemptions from State Registration, p. 51

items.x: Same jurisdictional logic as the firm: an agent registers in any state where the agent has a place of business, OR where the agent has clients who are residents — unless a narrow exclusion applies.
Snowbird: an agent with no place of business in a state may continue to deal with an EXISTING customer who is temporarily present there and remains a resident of another state.
Two things snowbird never covers: soliciting a new customer in the temporary state, and directing advertising into it. The relationship must predate the travel.

An agent’s registration is not effective during any period when the agent is not associated with a registered broker-dealer or a registered issuer. The license does not travel with the person between jobs — it goes dormant.
When an agent begins or terminates a connection with a broker-dealer or issuer, BOTH the agent and the firm must notify the Administrator.

“The agent is registered in New York, so she may service a New York client who has retired to Florida.” True only if the client remains a non-resident temporarily present in Florida. A client who has MOVED to Florida is a Florida resident, and snowbird does not apply.

cells.title: Registration mechanics
refs: STC 43e Ch. 3 General Registration of Financial Professionals, p. 40; Managers as Agents, p. 52

items.x: The application is Form U4, filed by the FIRM — not by the individual — electronically through the Central Registration Depository. It collects identity, residential and employment history, examination and registration history, outside business activities, and disclosure of criminal, regulatory, civil judicial, customer complaint, termination, and financial events. Fingerprints are submitted for a federal criminal background check.
A separate Form U4 is required for each firm the individual is registered with. The registration belongs to the relationship, not to the person alone.
As with firms, an agent’s registration becomes effective at noon on the thirtieth day after filing, expires December 31, and requires a consent to service of process and a fee.

Automatic registration. When a broker-dealer’s registration in a state first becomes effective, its partners, officers, and directors who effect securities transactions are automatically registered as agents in that state. They still file a Form U4 but need not take a qualification examination.

Two edges on that rule, both tested. It reaches only those actually involved in effecting securities transactions — a founding chief financial officer who handles only the firm’s books is not automatically registered. And it applies only at the firm’s INITIAL registration — someone promoted into an officer role two years later must complete the whole process: Form U4, examination, fee.
The Administrator may require an applicant to pass a written or oral examination, and may require a minimum period of experience.

cells.title: Maintaining registration
refs: STC 43e Ch. 3 Post-Registration Requirements for Agents, p. 53

items.x: Form U4 must be amended within 30 days of any event requiring disclosure. Address and name changes, criminal charges and convictions, regulatory actions, investment-related civil judgments, bankruptcies, liens and compromises with creditors, new outside business activities, and customer complaints alleging sales practice violations all trigger it.

Form U5 is filed by the FIRM within 30 days of the agent’s termination, stating the reason and disclosing any open allegations or investigations. For two years after filing, the former firm must amend the U5 with new information that comes to light about the person’s conduct during their tenure.
The two-year U5 window is a DISCLOSURE obligation, not a supervisory one. The old firm does not keep supervising the person; it keeps telling the truth about what happened while it did.

An agent may be registered with more than one broker-dealer at the same time, with written approval from each firm and a separate Form U4 for each. Supervisory responsibility stays firm-by-firm and does not transfer.
“The agent files the U5.” Wrong — the firm files both the U4 and the U5.

cells.title: How a registration ends
refs: STC 43e Ch. 7 Administrative Actions Associated with Registration, p. 141; Cancellations and Withdrawals, p. 145

items.x: Four endings, and the exam cares about which are punitive and which are not. Denial, suspension, and revocation are sanctions and require a finding of cause. Withdrawal and cancellation are not sanctions and involve no allegation of wrongdoing.

Grounds for denial, suspension, or revocation include: a false or misleading statement in the application · willful violation of the Act or a rule or order · conviction within the past ten years of a securities-related misdemeanor or any felony · a permanent or temporary injunction from any court against securities-related conduct · an order by another state’s securities administrator or by the SEC · engaging in dishonest or unethical practices · insolvency · lack of qualification by training, experience, or knowledge · failure to pay the filing fee. In each case the action must also be in the PUBLIC INTEREST — cause alone is not enough.

CANCELLATION is the Administrator’s housekeeping tool. It applies when a registrant no longer exists, has ceased doing business, cannot be located after reasonable search, or has been declared mentally incompetent. The classic fact pattern is mail returned with no forwarding address — the answer is cancel, not revoke.
WITHDRAWAL is voluntary and effective in thirty days, with the Administrator retaining jurisdiction for one year afterward.

Due process for the punitive actions: prior written notice, an opportunity for a hearing, and written findings of fact and conclusions of law. The Administrator may act summarily — postponing or suspending pending final determination — but must then notify the parties promptly and, on written request, hold a hearing within fifteen days.

A stem describing death, disappearance, dissolution, or incapacity is asking about cancellation. A stem describing misconduct is asking about denial, suspension, or revocation. Mixing them up is the most reliable way to lose this question.

Lack of qualification is a limited ground. refs: STC 43e Ch. 6 Outside Securities Accounts, p. 107; Selling Away, p. 110

chapters.name: Regulation of Investment Advisers
chapters.spine: Three letters and three questions. Is the person an adviser at all — the ABC test. If yes, does an exclusion pull them back out. If they are still an adviser, do they answer to the SEC or to the state? Only three questions come from here, so learn it precisely and move on rather than sinking an evening into assets-under-management arithmetic the exam rarely asks for.

cells.title: The ABC test
refs: Achievable Ch. 1 Definitions — Investment advisers; 2.3 Investment advisers
STC 43e Ch. 4 General Registration of Investment Advisers, p. 63

items.x: An investment adviser is a person who, for compensation, engages in the business of advising others as to the value of securities or the advisability of investing in, purchasing, or selling securities — or who, as part of a regular business, issues analyses or reports concerning securities. Collapse that into three prongs.
A — Advice about SECURITIES. B — in the BUSINESS of giving it. C — for COMPENSATION. All three must be present. Any one missing and the person is not an adviser.

Each prong has a live edge. Advice must be about securities, so generic budgeting, insurance-only advice, commodities, and direct real estate all fail prong A. Being in the business means holding out as an adviser or advising regularly — an occasional favor fails prong B. Compensation need not be cash, need not be labeled an advisory fee, and need not come from the client; anything of economic value satisfies prong C. A firm that advises another firm in exchange for legal services has been compensated.

“The adviser was not paid separately for the advice, so there is no compensation.” Careful — indirect and bundled compensation counts. This is exactly how a wrap fee converts a broker-dealer into an adviser (see ETH-8).

The exam’s favorite target is prong A. Someone advising exclusively on fixed annuities, whole life, or physical gold is not giving advice about securities, so no amount of business regularity or compensation makes them an adviser.

cells.title: Exclusions from the definition
refs: STC 43e Ch. 4 Exclusions from the Definition of a State Investment Adviser, p. 73

items.x: Passing the ABC test is not the end. Certain persons are excluded outright, on the theory that they are already regulated elsewhere or their advice is a byproduct of some other work.
Banks, savings institutions, and trust companies. The exclusion covers the institution itself — not a separately organized advisory subsidiary or affiliate.
Lawyers, accountants, teachers, and engineers whose performance of advisory services is SOLELY INCIDENTAL to the practice of their profession.
Broker-dealers and their agents whose advisory services are solely incidental to the conduct of their brokerage business AND who receive NO SPECIAL COMPENSATION for the advice.

Note the asymmetry, because a question can isolate it. The special-compensation condition is written into the broker-dealer exclusion. The professionals’ exclusion turns on “solely incidental” alone. In practice a separately billed advisory fee usually destroys “solely incidental” as well, so the working heuristic — any separate charge for advice kills the exclusion — is safe. Know the statutory split as the tiebreaker.
Publishers of bona fide newspapers, news magazines, and business or financial publications of general and regular circulation.

The publisher exclusion is destroyed by personalization. A general-circulation newsletter with the same content for every subscriber is excluded; one that tailors recommendations to individual subscribers’ circumstances is not, and the publisher must register.

Also excluded: persons whose only clients are insurance companies · federal covered advisers, which are excluded from STATE registration · and any other person the Administrator designates by rule or order.
“A broker-dealer can never be an investment adviser.” Wrong — the moment it charges a separate fee for advice, the exclusion is gone and it must register.

cells.title: Exemptions from state registration — de minimis
refs: STC 43e Ch. 4 Exemptions from State Registration, p. 75

items.x: An exclusion means the person is not an adviser at all. An exemption means they are an adviser but need not register in a particular state. Keep the words apart; the exam sometimes tests the distinction directly.

The de minimis exemption has TWO prongs and both must be satisfied: no place of business in the state, AND no more than five non-institutional clients who are residents of the state during the preceding twelve months.

Institutional clients do not count toward the five. Other investment advisers, broker-dealers, banks, insurance companies, investment companies, and large pension plans are outside the tally. An adviser with fifty institutional clients and four retail clients in a state, and no office there, is exempt.
Any place of business in the state destroys the exemption regardless of client count. One in-state office and zero clients still means registration.

Contrast with the broker-dealer rule, which the exam pairs deliberately: there is NO de minimis for broker-dealers. One in-state retail customer forces registration. Advisers get five; broker-dealers get none.

cells.title: The federal-state dividing line
refs: STC 43e Ch. 4 Investment Advisers Act of 1940, p. 76; Federal Covered Advisers, p. 77

items.x: A federal covered adviser registers with and is regulated by the SEC, and the state is preempted from requiring its registration. What the state keeps is a notice filing with a fee, the registration of the adviser’s in-state IARs, and full antifraud authority. What it loses is the power to impose registration, books-and-records, financial, or supervisory requirements on the firm.

Federal covered status: must register with the SEC at $110 million or more in assets under management · may register between $100 and $110 million · must withdraw from SEC registration if assets fall below $90 million · an adviser to a registered investment company is federal covered at any size · an adviser required to register in fifteen or more states may register federally · pension consultants qualify at $200 million or more.

The buffer between $90 and $110 million exists so advisers are not forced to switch regulators every time markets move. The exam rarely asks the numbers themselves; it asks what being federal covered costs the state.
A notice filing by a federal covered adviser consists of a copy of the Form ADV filed with the SEC, a consent to service of process, and the state fee.
“A federal covered adviser has nothing to do with the state.” Wrong on three counts — notice filing, IAR registration, and antifraud jurisdiction all survive.

cells.title: Form ADV and the brochure rule
refs: STC 43e Ch. 4 Form ADV Part 1, p. 63; Part 2A — The Brochure Rule, p. 64; Part 2B, p. 66; Updates and Amendments, p. 67

items.x: One form carries the whole adviser registration system, and the axis every question turns on is filed-with-the-regulator versus delivered-to-the-client.

Part 1 — structured data about the adviser: ownership, control persons, clients, assets under management, advisory activities, affiliations, custody arrangements, disciplinary history. Filed with the regulator. Never delivered to clients.
Part 2A — the BROCHURE. A plain-English narrative describing services, fees, conflicts, methods of analysis, disciplinary information, brokerage practices, and custody. Delivered to clients.
Part 2B — the brochure SUPPLEMENT, covering the specific individual who will advise the client: education, business background, disciplinary events, other business activities. Delivered to clients.

Delivery by a STATE-REGISTERED adviser: either not less than 48 HOURS before entering the advisory contract, OR at the time of entering the contract provided the client may terminate without penalty within FIVE BUSINESS DAYS. It is an either/or, not a both.
During that five-business-day free-look window the adviser may charge for services actually rendered but may not impose a cancellation penalty. After the window, ordinary termination terms apply.
Delivery by a FEDERAL COVERED adviser: at or before entering the contract. There is no free-look alternative at the federal level.
No brochure need be delivered to a registered investment company client, or where the contract is for impersonal advisory services costing the client less than $500 a year.

Annually, the adviser must deliver either an updated brochure or a summary of material changes, within 120 days of its fiscal year end. Form ADV is amended annually within 90 days of fiscal year end, and promptly whenever information becomes materially inaccurate.
“Part 2A is filed but not delivered.” Wrong — Part 2A IS the brochure. Part 1 is the one that never goes to clients.

cells.title: Advisory contracts
refs: Achievable 2.3 Investment advisers; 4.3 Customer funds & securities
STC 43e Ch. 4 Investment Advisory Contracts, p. 82

items.x: Every advisory contract must be IN WRITING and must set out: the services to be provided · the term of the contract · the advisory fee and the formula for computing it · the amount of any prepaid fee to be returned on early termination · whether the contract grants discretionary authority · that the contract may not be assigned without the client’s consent · and, for an adviser organized as a partnership, that the adviser will notify clients of any change in partnership membership within a reasonable time.

Assignment reaches further than a formal transfer of paper. A change in CONTROL of the advisory firm — the sale of the practice, a change in majority ownership — is an assignment. Clients are not inventory and do not convey with the business; each must consent.

Performance-based fees are generally prohibited, because they give the adviser an incentive to take risk the client did not ask for. The main exception permits them where the client is a qualified client, tested by assets under management with the adviser or by net worth. The current thresholds were raised by inflation adjustment effective June 29, 2026 to $1.4 million in assets under management or more than $2.7 million in net worth, from $1.1 million and $2.2 million; contracts entered before that date are grandfathered.

“The fee was reasonable, so the contract is fine.” Reasonableness is not the test for the required contents. A contract missing the fee formula, the prepaid-fee refund term, or the assignment clause is defective no matter how fair the pricing.

cells.title: Custody and financial requirements
refs: STC 43e Ch. 4 Custody, p. 70; Minimum Financial Requirements, p. 70; Custody of Client Funds and Securities, p. 84

items.x: Custody means holding client funds or securities directly or indirectly, or having any authority to obtain possession of them. The clean diagnostic: can the adviser get money OUT of the account? If yes, custody. Deducting an advisory fee directly from a client account counts.

Additional state triggers: inadvertently receiving client funds or securities and holding them more than THREE BUSINESS DAYS · accepting a third-party check and holding it more than three business days · serving as general partner of a limited partnership whose assets the adviser can reach.
The three-business-day rule is why the answer to “a client hands you a check payable to a fund” is always forward it promptly. Holding it is what creates the problem; the receipt itself does not.

An Administrator may by rule PROHIBIT advisers from taking custody entirely. Where custody is permitted, the adviser must notify the Administrator in writing that it has custody, must use a qualified custodian, must arrange for the custodian to send account statements to clients at least quarterly, and is subject to an annual surprise examination by an independent accountant.

Minimum financial requirements: $35,000 net worth for an adviser with custody · $10,000 for an adviser with discretionary authority but no custody · an adviser that accepts prepayment of more than $500 in fees six or more months in advance must maintain positive net worth.

If net worth falls below the minimum: notify the Administrator by the close of the NEXT business day, and file a financial report by the close of the business day AFTER that. A shortfall may be cured by posting a surety bond equal to the deficiency, rounded up to the nearest $5,000.

An adviser can avoid custody entirely by having a qualified custodian — a bank or broker-dealer — hold client cash and securities. That is the ordinary structure and it is why most advisory firms carry the $10,000 requirement rather than the $35,000 one.

cells.title: Recordkeeping and privacy
refs: STC 43e Ch. 4 State Recordkeeping Requirements, p. 72; Ch. 6 Confidentiality of Client Information, p. 120; Cyber Security and Data Protection, p. 125

items.x: Adviser records: kept for FIVE years from the end of the fiscal year in which the last entry was made, with the first TWO years in the adviser’s principal office. Partnership articles, corporate charters, minute books, and stock certificate books are kept three years after termination of the enterprise.

Do not confuse this with the broker-dealer clocks. Broker-dealer customer account records run six years; adviser records run five. The “first two years easily accessible” language appears in both, which is exactly why the swap works as a distractor.
A state may not impose recordkeeping requirements on a federal covered adviser — preempted, like net capital and bonding.

Privacy sits on two layers. The federal rule requires a firm to give each customer an initial privacy notice no later than when the relationship is established, an annual notice while it continues, a clear opportunity to opt out of sharing nonpublic personal information with non-affiliated third parties, and written policies safeguarding customer records against unauthorized access.

The parallel state model rule for advisers requires written policies and procedures reasonably designed to ensure the security and confidentiality of client records, to protect against anticipated threats, and to protect against unauthorized access that could cause substantial harm or inconvenience — plus DELIVERY of the privacy policy to clients and retention of records of that delivery.

chapters.name: Regulation of Investment Adviser Representatives
chapters.spine: The firm and the individual register separately and always independently. The firm’s registration follows its business; the individual’s follows their offices. Get that asymmetry and three questions become free points.

cells.title: Definition — the five activities
refs: Achievable Ch. 1 Definitions — Investment adviser representatives; 2.4
STC 43e Ch. 4 Registration of Investment Adviser Representatives, p. 78

items.x: An investment adviser representative is any partner, officer, director, or other individual associated with an investment adviser who does any ONE of the following: makes recommendations or renders advice about securities · manages accounts or portfolios of clients · determines which recommendation or advice should be given · solicits, offers, or negotiates for the sale of investment advisory services · supervises employees who do any of those.
Any one is enough. The five verbs — recommend, manage, determine, solicit, supervise — map the full lifecycle of an advisory engagement, and the definition is satisfied at any point along it.
The fifth verb catches people. A back-office supervisor who never speaks to a client but oversees IARs is an IAR. Client contact is not the test; the five activities are.

The third verb catches a different group: the research analyst who never meets a client but decides what the firm will recommend. Determining the advice is IAR activity even when someone else delivers it.

refs: STC 43e Ch. 4 Registration of Investment Adviser Representatives, p. 78

items.x: An employee whose duties are purely clerical or ministerial is not an IAR. Same functional logic as the agent-side exclusion, and it fails in the same place.

The exclusion dies on: making a specific recommendation to a client, even from a script and even under supervision · soliciting a prospective client to engage the firm · negotiating advisory contracts or fees · holding oneself out to the public as an investment professional.
“The recommendation was scripted and approved, so the employee was not really advising.” Wrong — scripts and supervision do not launder the activity.

cells.title: Where the IAR registers
refs: $2 Textbook Mod 2, Lesson 13 · p. 40; Lesson 14 · p. 41

cells.title: De minimis for IARs
refs: STC 43e Ch. 4 Representatives of State-Registered Investment Advisers, pp. 78–80

cells.title: Registration mechanics
refs: STC 43e Ch. 4 Registration of IARs, p. 78; Statutory Disqualifications from Registration, p. 81

items.x: The IAR files Form U4 through the CRD/IARD system, with fingerprints, a consent to service of process, and the state fee. Registration becomes effective at noon on the thirtieth day and expires December 31, on the same clocks as every other person registration.
Form U4 must be amended within 30 days of any material change: address, name, disciplinary events, outside business activities, financial disclosures.

cells.title: IAR, agent, or both
refs: Achievable 2.4 Investment adviser representatives; 4.1 Standards of care

items.x: Dual registration is common and entirely permissible: the same individual may be an agent of a broker-dealer and an IAR of an investment adviser. What changes is the standard of care, and it changes by the hour depending on which hat is being worn.

Compensation must be disclosed in each capacity, and a client may not be charged an advisory fee and a brokerage commission on the same transaction without both being disclosed.

The IAR’s side of that bargain: cooperate with compliance, report material events and complaints promptly, disclose outside business activities, and adhere to firm policy on personal trading, gifts, and confidentiality.

chapters.name: Communication with Customers and Prospects
chapters.spine: Twelve questions, and they come in two flavors. Half hand you a sentence and ask whether saying it is lawful. Half name an account type and ask which document, which agreement, which approval, in what order. The first half is about three forbidden claims; the second is a matching exercise. Neither requires much reasoning — but both punish imprecision hard.

cells.title: Required disclosures
refs: STC 43e Ch. 4 Form ADV Part 2, p. 64; Ch. 6 Communications with Clients, p. 120

items.x: Disclosure obligations divide by what is being disclosed: facts about the product, facts about the relationship, and facts about changes in either.

Product disclosures: the material risks of a recommended security · fees and expenses, including sales charges, ongoing distribution fees, and management fees · conflicts of interest connected to the product · tax consequences where material.

Relationship disclosures: the client relationship summary at the start of a retail relationship · the adviser brochure and brochure supplement · the terms of the advisory or brokerage agreement · the firm’s and the individual’s disciplinary history.

Changed-circumstances disclosures: any change in the firm’s financial condition that could impair its ability to meet commitments to clients · new disciplinary events · material changes to the brochure.

The unifying test for whether something must be disclosed is materiality: would a reasonable investor consider it important in making the decision? That single question resolves most disclosure fact patterns without any list at all.

cells.title: Registration is not approval
refs: STC 43e Ch. 6 False and Misleading Statements, p. 99

items.x: This is the counterintuitive one, which is exactly why it is tested so often. Registration — of a person, a firm, or a security, with a state or with the SEC — confers no endorsement whatsoever. It does not mean the regulator reviewed the merits, vouched for the quality of the advice, or verified the accuracy of the disclosure. Representing otherwise is unlawful.

Always prohibited: claiming registration ensures quality · claiming a security or strategy has been approved by the SEC or the state · offering registration as assurance of integrity · any phrasing that turns a registration status into a credential.

Always permitted: stating the plain fact of registration — registered with the SEC as an investment adviser, registered in this state as a broker-dealer, a registered representative of this firm since a given year.
The line runs between stating the status and selling it. And no disclaimer rescues an implied endorsement; the prohibition reaches indirect implications and fine print as squarely as direct claims.
When a stem asks which of four statements about registration is permitted, look for the one that is purely factual and makes no claim about quality, safety, or approval.

cells.title: Performance guarantees
refs: STC 43e Ch. 6 Guaranteeing Clients a Profit, p. 107

items.x: No representation may guarantee future investment performance or protect against loss. The rule covers written and oral statements and it covers implication as well as assertion.

Prohibited: promising a rate of return · promising outperformance · saying the client cannot lose principal or that the money is safe · citing an unbroken record of positive years in a way that implies it will continue, even if the record is literally true · an agent personally promising to make the customer whole on a loss.

Permitted, because they are specific true statements about a specific product with a named guarantor: direct obligations of the U.S. Treasury are backed by the full faith and credit of the United States · deposits at an insured institution are federally insured up to the applicable limit · a named third party guarantees a particular bond.

Recall the statutory meaning of “guaranteed” from SEC-3: guaranteed as to principal, interest, or dividends, by someone other than the issuer. Capital gains are never guaranteed. And a guarantee is only as good as the guarantor — a parent guaranteeing a subsidiary’s bonds does not eliminate credit risk.
Reimbursing a client for a loss out of the agent’s own pocket is prohibited, and so is the promise to do it. Both are treated as guarantees against loss.

You will find this rule sits uncomfortably close to how principal-protected structured notes are actually marketed. The state-law answer is cruder than your professional vocabulary: unless the guarantee is a specific, named, true third-party obligation, describing a product as protected against loss is a violation.

refs: STC 43e Ch. 3 Client Accounts and Orders, p. 56; New Customer Accounts, p. 56; Individual / Joint / TOD Accounts, pp. 57–58

items.x: Required for EVERY account: the customer’s name and residence address · whether the customer is of legal age · tax identification number · occupation and the name and address of the employer · the signature of the registered representative responsible for the account · the signature of a principal signifying acceptance.

Additionally required where the firm will make recommendations: annual income · net worth and liquid net worth · investment objectives · risk tolerance · time horizon and liquidity needs · other holdings, investment experience, and tax status.

Maintenance cadence: the recorded account information must be sent to the customer within 30 days of opening and at least every 36 months thereafter, with any material changes the customer reports incorporated. Account records are retained at least six years after the account is closed.

A principal must approve every new account before the first order is entered. A principal is not required to approve each order ticket before entry — orders are reviewed after execution. That before/after split is testable.

“The customer declined to provide net worth, so the account cannot be opened.” Not quite — the account can be opened; what the firm cannot do is make recommendations without a reasonable basis to judge suitability.

A margin account lets the customer borrow part of the purchase price from the firm with the securities as collateral. Two regulators split the job: the Federal Reserve sets what must be deposited at the moment of purchase, and the self-regulatory rules govern every day afterward.
Initial margin is 50% of the purchase price for marginable equity securities, long or short. Minimum equity to open is $2,000, or 100% of the purchase price if the security costs less than $2,000.
Maintenance margin: 25% of market value for long positions, 30% for short positions in stock priced $5 or more. Firms may impose higher house requirements.

Three agreements: the CREDIT or margin agreement, which sets the lending terms and the firm’s right to liquidate — required. The HYPOTHECATION agreement, permitting the firm to pledge the customer’s securities as collateral for its own borrowing — required. The LOAN CONSENT agreement, permitting the firm to lend the customer’s securities to third parties — OPTIONAL.
Only the loan consent is optional. A question offering “all three are required” or “the hypothecation agreement is optional” is testing exactly this.
Not everything is marginable. New issues are not marginable for 30 days, and options must be paid for in full.
A maintenance call is satisfied by depositing cash or marginable securities — not by buying more stock, which increases the requirement rather than meeting it.

cells.title: Options accounts and options valuation
refs: STC 43e Ch. 3 Option Accounts, p. 59; Ch. 6 Options, p. 130

items.x: The paperwork sequence, in order: collect the customer’s profile including options-specific experience and objectives → deliver the options disclosure document at or before the time the account is approved → a registered options principal approves the account → the signed options agreement comes back within 15 DAYS of approval.
If the signed agreement does not arrive within 15 days, the account is not frozen — it is restricted to CLOSING transactions only. Existing positions may be unwound; nothing new may be opened.
The disclosure document is DELIVERED, not signed. The options AGREEMENT is the document signed and returned within 15 days. Swapping those two is the standard distractor.

Valuation is tested at vocabulary depth only. A premium has exactly two components: intrinsic value, which is the amount by which the option is in the money, and time value, which is everything else. Intrinsic value is never negative — it is either positive or zero.

A CALL is in the money when the market price is ABOVE the strike. A PUT is in the money when the market price is BELOW the strike. At the money means market equals strike. Out of the money means no intrinsic value, so the entire premium is time value.

One subtraction is the whole skill: time value equals premium minus intrinsic value. A $50-strike call with the stock at $54 has $4 of intrinsic value; if the premium is $5.50, time value is $1.50. Drop the stock to $48 and intrinsic value is zero, so the entire remaining premium is time value.

This is well below the depth you already carry from structured products work. Resist the urge to over-answer — the exam is not asking about greeks, volatility, or path dependency, and no answer choice will reward that knowledge.

refs: STC 43e Ch. 3 Advertising and Sales Literature, p. 43; Ch. 6 Communications with the Public, p. 118; Social Media, pp. 121–124

items.x: Federal communication rules sort every message into one of three categories, and the sorting is done by AUDIENCE and VOLUME — never by medium. A tweet, an email, and a television advertisement can land in three different categories depending on who sees them.
RETAIL COMMUNICATION — distributed or made available to more than 25 retail investors within any 30 calendar-day period. Requires principal approval before first use, with limited exceptions.
CORRESPONDENCE — 25 or fewer retail investors within any 30 calendar-day period. No pre-use approval; the firm supervises by reviewing a representative sample under written procedures.
INSTITUTIONAL COMMUNICATION — distributed only to institutional investors. No pre-use approval; written procedures and sample review instead.

Filing: certain retail communications must be filed 10 business days BEFORE first use — including those about closed-end funds during the offering period and those containing certain performance rankings. Most other retail communications about registered investment companies and public direct participation programs are filed within 10 business days AFTER first use. Institutional communications and correspondence are not filed.

Content standards apply to all three categories: no false or misleading statements, no predictions or projections of performance, fair and balanced treatment of risks and benefits, and required disclosures where relevant.

Social media follows the same sorting. Static content — a profile, a biography, a posted advertisement — is normally retail communication and needs pre-use approval. Interactive content — live replies, real-time comments — is normally correspondence and is supervised by review. All business-related electronic communication must be captured and retained, wherever it happens; if the firm cannot archive a channel, business may not be conducted there.

Layered on top, from state law: advertising and sales literature relating to registered securities must be FILED with the Administrator. Advertising means any written communication addressed to more than one person, and a firm’s website qualifies.
“A static social media post is correspondence.” Wrong — static content is advertising-style and is normally a retail communication. Interactive replies are the correspondence side.

Retention — LIFETIME of the firm plus two years: partnership articles, corporate charters, minute books, stock certificate books.
Retention — SIX years, first two easily accessible: customer account records, blotters, general ledgers, securities records.

Retention — THREE years, first two easily accessible: order tickets, trade confirmations, communications with the public, trial balances, and customer complaints. Forms BD, U4, and U5 are kept at least three years after termination.
Electronic storage must be non-rewritable and non-erasable, or otherwise satisfy audit-trail requirements, and records must be producible to examiners on demand.
