chapters.name: Ethical Practices and Obligations
chapters.spine: The largest single subject on the exam, and the most predictable. Regulators think in named violations, and so does the exam: it describes a behavior and asks you to name it, or names a behavior and asks who could have committed it. Learn the four drawers — manipulation, misrepresentation, account abuse, personal conduct — and learn the actor attached to each item. Then learn the protective rules bolted on top.

cells.title: The antifraud spine and the three standards of care
refs: Achievable 4.1 Standards of care; Ch. 3 Enforcement
STC 43e Ch. 2 Anti-Fraud Provisions, p. 37; Ch. 3 Regulation Best Interest, p. 56; Ch. 5 Fiduciary Duty, p. 89; Suitability Obligations, p. 93

items.x: The state antifraud provision makes it unlawful, in connection with the offer, sale, OR PURCHASE of any security, to employ any device or scheme to defraud, to make an untrue statement of a material fact or omit a material fact necessary to make statements not misleading, or to engage in any act or practice that operates as a fraud or deceit.

Three features of that sentence get tested. It covers PURCHASES as well as sales — defrauding someone into selling you their stock cheaply is squarely within it. It reaches offers, so a transaction need never close. And it applies to every security and every person, with no exemption available to anyone, ever.

A parallel provision covers investment advice: it is unlawful for a person advising others for compensation to employ any scheme to defraud a client, or to engage in any practice that operates as a fraud on a client.
Layered on top are three standards of care, and the exam expects them kept surgically apart. Read the ACTOR first, then the MOMENT.

FIDUCIARY DUTY — owed by investment advisers and IARs. Continuous, not point-of-sale. Requires loyalty, care, full disclosure of material conflicts, and placing the client’s interest ahead of the firm’s. Survives the recommendation and runs for the life of the relationship.

BEST INTEREST — owed by broker-dealers and their agents when making a recommendation to a retail customer. It attaches AT the recommendation and runs on four obligations: care, disclosure, conflict of interest, and compliance.

SUITABILITY — the older standard, governing recommendations not covered by the best-interest rule. Three prongs: reasonable-basis (the product is suitable for someone), customer-specific (it suits THIS customer’s profile), and quantitative (the pattern of recommendations is not excessive).

The tell in the stem is usually the noun and the timing. A question naming “the investment adviser” and describing an ongoing obligation — monitoring, review, throughout the relationship — is a fiduciary question. One naming “the registered representative” at the moment of a trade is a best-interest question.

“Suitability applies whenever the firm has a customer.” Wrong — suitability and the best-interest obligation attach at a RECOMMENDATION. Where there is no recommendation, only the antifraud and fair-dealing duties apply.

cells.title: Market manipulation and insider trading
refs: STC 43e Ch. 6 Use of Insider Information, p. 101; Market Manipulation, p. 108

items.x: Manipulation is lying to the market with orders instead of words — creating a false impression of supply, demand, price, or volume. Each named practice has a tell, and the tell is the answer.
SPOOFING — entering bids or offers with the intent to cancel before execution. Tell: intent to cancel.
LAYERING — spoofing at multiple price levels with a series of non-bona-fide orders. Tell: multiple layers, none genuine.
FRONT-RUNNING — trading ahead of a known pending customer order to profit from the price move it will cause. Tell: trading ahead of customer flow.
WASH SALES and MATCHED ORDERS — transactions producing no real change in beneficial ownership, arranged to manufacture apparent activity. Tell: no change of ownership.
PUMP AND DUMP — spreading false favorable information to inflate a price, then selling into the demand created. Tell: promotion followed by the promoter selling.

The publication side: a firm may not publish or circulate, or cause to be circulated, any communication reporting a transaction as a purchase or sale unless it believes the trade was bona fide, or quoting a bid or offer unless it believes the quotation is bona fide. Tell: publicizing prices or volume the firm does not believe are real.

Insider trading is fraud committed with information rather than with orders. Two words carry it — the information must be MATERIAL (a reasonable investor would consider it important) and NON-PUBLIC (not yet widely disseminated).

Liability reaches the whole chain: the person who trades on the information, the person who tips it even without trading, the person who receives the tip and trades, and the firm that failed to supervise. Firms manage this with information barriers between departments holding non-public information and their trading desks.
“The tipper did not trade, so the tipper is not liable.” Wrong — tipping is itself a violation.

cells.title: Misrepresentation, omission, and the bank-premises rules
refs: STC 43e Ch. 6 False and Misleading Statements, p. 99; Securities Transactions on Bank Premises, p. 117

items.x: Fraud has two grammatical forms and they carry equal weight: saying something false, and omitting the fact that would have made the rest of it not misleading. Nothing in the Act ranks omission below assertion.

Named misrepresentations: guarantees of return or against loss · claims that registration confers approval · statements about a fund that contradict or exceed the prospectus, including hypothetical performance and projected returns · misleading use of titles or credentials, including designations implying expertise in advising seniors that were issued by an organization with no meaningful standards · misstating the status of a customer’s account or the price of a security.

A professional designation may be used only if it was issued by an accredited organization with real qualification standards, continuing education, and a public disciplinary process; was not awarded merely for paying a fee or attending a marketing session; and is not used in a way that misleads investors about the holder’s expertise.

When securities are sold on the premises of a bank, savings institution, or credit union, customers must receive four disclosures — in writing at account opening and orally at the time of any recommendation.

The four bank-premises disclosures: the securities are NOT federally insured · they are NOT a deposit or other obligation of the institution · they are NOT guaranteed by the institution · they ARE subject to investment risk, including possible loss of principal.

Additionally: the securities sales area must be physically distinct from the deposit-taking area wherever practicable, signage must be displayed, and the institution must maintain written customer-complaint procedures.

The rule exists to police one specific confusion — customers mistaking an investment product for an insured deposit because of where they bought it. Keep that purpose in mind and the four disclosures reconstruct themselves.

cells.title: Account abuse
refs: STC 43e Ch. 4 Discretionary Authority, p. 69; Ch. 6 Making Unsuitable Recommendations, p. 103; Exercising Discretion without Written Authority, p. 113

items.x: CHURNING — trading excessively in a customer’s account relative to the customer’s objectives and resources, to generate commissions. Examined through turnover ratio, cost-to-equity ratio, and whether the pattern makes sense for the stated objectives. It is the quantitative suitability prong made concrete.

UNAUTHORIZED TRANSACTIONS — trades placed without the customer’s prior consent, except in an account where written discretionary authority has been granted. Good faith is not a defense; a profitable unauthorized trade is still a violation.

UNSUITABLE RECOMMENDATIONS — recommending securities inconsistent with the customer’s objectives, financial situation, or needs, including recommending purchases beyond the customer’s financial capability.

Discretion abuse deserves its own treatment because the rule differs by actor, and the exam exploits that. A BROKER-DEALER or agent must have WRITTEN discretionary authority in hand BEFORE exercising discretion — there is no grace period. An INVESTMENT ADVISER or IAR may act on ORAL authority for up to TEN BUSINESS DAYS from the first discretionary transaction, and must obtain written authority by the end of that period.
Discretion exists when the professional decides any one of three things without contacting the client: the ACTION (buy or sell), the ASSET (which security), or the AMOUNT. Any one is enough.

If the client specifies action, asset, and amount and leaves only PRICE and/or TIME to the professional, that is not discretion — it is a not-held order. No written authority is required, and the order is good only for the day it is entered.
“An agent may act on oral discretion for ten business days.” Wrong — that window belongs to investment advisers only.
“A not-held order stays open until executed.” Wrong — day only.

Also prohibited: effecting transactions not recorded on the firm’s books unless authorized in writing · exercising discretion without authority · failing to follow a customer’s instruction about their own account.

cells.title: Investment company share abuses
refs: STC 43e Ch. 6 NASAA Statement of Policy … Investment Company Shares, pp. 115–116

items.x: Mutual fund sales get their own catalogue of named practices because the fee structures create specific opportunities for abuse. Each one is tested as a fact pattern where you name the violation.

BREAKPOINT SALES — recommending or accepting an investment just below the amount that would qualify for a reduced sales charge, without informing the customer that a slightly larger investment would cost proportionally less.
FAILURE TO OFFER A LETTER OF INTENT — not informing a customer that a letter of intent would let them reach a breakpoint by aggregating purchases over 13 months.
SHARE-CLASS ABUSE — recommending a higher-cost class when the customer qualifies for or would be better served by a lower-cost one.
SWITCHING — recommending the sale of one fund to buy another, principally to generate a new sales charge, where the funds have substantially similar objectives.

SELLING DIVIDENDS — telling or implying that buying fund shares shortly before the ex-dividend date is advantageous. It is not: the net asset value drops by the distribution amount, so the buyer receives part of their own purchase price back and owes tax on it immediately. A second prong of the same violation is implying that a long-term capital gains distribution is part of the fund’s income yield — it is a distribution of appreciation, not recurring income.

Every one of these turns on the sales pitch rather than the product. The fund itself may be perfectly suitable; misrepresenting why or how to buy it is what creates the violation.

cells.title: Violations only a firm can commit
refs: STC 43e Ch. 6 Commingling, p. 104; Withholding Sales of IPO Shares, p. 111; Unnecessarily Delaying Payments or Deliveries, p. 112; Executing Orders at Unfair Prices, p. 113; Charging Excessive Fees, p. 113

items.x: Several named practices are operational failures that only a broker-dealer, not an individual, is in a position to commit. The exam tests this by asking what the FIRM did wrong, and plants agent-only items as distractors.

DELIVERY DELAYS — a pattern of unreasonable and unjustifiable delay in delivering securities a customer has purchased, or in paying out a free credit balance on request. A free credit balance is the customer’s uninvested cash and must be remitted when asked.

DISHONORING QUOTES, sometimes called backing away — quoting a price at which the firm is not actually prepared to trade. A firm quoting a two-sided market must stand ready to trade at those prices, at least for the minimum quantity, under the stated conditions.

UNREASONABLE SERVICE FEES — charging unreasonable or inequitable fees for miscellaneous services such as collecting dividends or interest, transferring or exchanging securities, appraisals, safekeeping, and custody. A firm offering more service may charge more, but the fee must be reasonable and disclosed.

WITHHOLDING SHARES OF A PUBLIC OFFERING — failing to make a bona fide public offering of all securities allotted to the firm in a distribution. Holding back shares of a hot issue for the firm, its officers, or its agents rather than allocating them fairly is the violation, whatever price the insiders pay.
COMMINGLING and IMPROPER HYPOTHECATION — mixing customer securities with the firm’s own, or pledging customer securities beyond what the customer’s indebtedness and agreements permit.

Two related practices reach both firm and agent. HIGHER-THAN-NORMAL COMMISSIONS on a thinly traded security can be legitimate — the offense is charging them without disclosing in advance. Undisclosed premium pricing, not premium pricing, is the violation. FREE-LUNCH SEMINARS marketed as education with assurances that nothing will be sold, where the real purpose is opening accounts, make both the sponsoring firm and the presenting agent responsible.

cells.title: Violations at the individual level
refs: STC 43e Ch. 6 Borrowing and Lending, p. 105; Sharing in the Profits or Losses in a Client’s Account, p. 106; Selling Away, p. 110

items.x: BORROWING FROM OR LENDING TO A CUSTOMER — prohibited unless the customer is a broker-dealer, an affiliate of the firm, or a financial institution in the business of lending. A long friendship, a family relationship, or the customer’s enthusiastic consent does not create an exception.

SHARING IN PROFITS AND LOSSES of a customer’s account — prohibited without prior written consent of BOTH the customer and the firm, and then only in proportion to the agent’s own capital contribution.

SPLITTING COMMISSIONS — an agent may divide compensation only with a person registered as an agent of the SAME broker-dealer, or of a broker-dealer under direct or indirect common control. Splitting with an agent of an unaffiliated firm, or with anyone unregistered, is prohibited. A permissible split ordinarily requires no disclosure to the client unless it increases the client’s cost.

FICTITIOUS ACCOUNT INFORMATION — establishing or maintaining an account containing false information in order to execute transactions that would otherwise be prohibited. The classic patterns are inflating a customer’s stated net worth to qualify the account for margin or options, and overstating investment experience to clear a suitability screen. The customer’s consent does not cure it; the false record is the violation.

SELLING AWAY — participating in a securities transaction outside the regular course of employment. Prior WRITTEN NOTICE to the firm is required in all cases regardless of compensation; where compensation is involved the firm must also approve and supervise. The transaction need not involve a firm customer to be a violation.

Contrast the disclosure logic on two of these, because the exam swaps them. Sharing in a customer’s profits and losses requires prior written consent from both customer and firm. A permissible commission split among affiliated agents requires no client disclosure at all.

The actor shortcut, which resolves a whole question type. FIRM ONLY: delivery delays, dishonoring quotes, unreasonable service fees, withholding shares of an offering, commingling. AGENT ONLY: splitting commissions outside the firm, fictitious account information, sharing in a customer’s account without consent. BOTH: churning, unauthorized trading, unsuitable recommendations, undisclosed premium charges, misleading statements, borrowing and lending outside permitted relationships. Check the actor before you check the conduct.

cells.title: Protective rules: vulnerable adults, conflicts, custody, and prudence
refs: Achievable 4.3 Customer funds & securities; 4.4 Unethical & criminal actions
$2 Textbook Mod 3, Lesson 5 · p. 58; Lesson 7 · pp. 64–66
STC 43e Ch. 5 The Uniform Prudent Investor Act, p. 90; Soft-Dollar Arrangements, p. 91; Ch. 6 Principal and Cross Trades, p. 119; Vulnerable Adults, p. 126

items.x: VULNERABLE ADULT — an individual 65 or older, or an adult protected under the state’s adult protective services statute.

TRUSTED CONTACT — firms must make reasonable efforts to obtain the name of a trusted contact person when opening an account. The client may decline. The trusted contact has NO authority over the account; they are an information resource the firm may reach if it suspects exploitation, suspects diminished capacity, or cannot reach the client.

TEMPORARY HOLDS — a firm that reasonably believes financial exploitation is occurring, has occurred, or is being attempted may place a temporary hold on a DISBURSEMENT. The initial hold runs up to 15 BUSINESS DAYS and may be extended by 10 more, for 25 total, if the firm’s internal review supports it. Notice must go to the Administrator and to adult protective services within 2 business days, and the firm must conduct an internal review.

Holds apply to disbursements, not to trading. Securities transactions inside the account continue. And any answer choice in which the trusted contact approves or directs something is wrong — they have no authority.

Red flags: sudden unexplained changes in financial patterns · a new friend or caregiver directing transactions · a client appearing confused or under duress · unusual wires to unfamiliar parties · unexplained changes to beneficiaries or powers of attorney.

Conflicts of interest divide into what disclosure can cure and what it cannot. It CANNOT cure: borrowing from or lending to clients, sharing in accounts without consent, trading or tipping on material non-public information, misappropriating client assets. It CAN permit, with full written disclosure: soft dollar arrangements within the statutory safe harbor, principal trades with prior written client consent, agency cross transactions, and outside business activities and accounts disclosed to the firm.

Best execution is still required, and the arrangements must be disclosed.

Permitted only with prior written client consent after written disclosure of the conflict and the compensation, a written confirmation at or before completion of each transaction, and an annual itemized report of all such transactions and total compensation. The condition no paperwork waives: the adviser may not have RECOMMENDED the transaction to both parties.

chapters.name: Remedies and Administrative Provisions
chapters.spine: One violation opens three separate doors: an administrative action by the Administrator, a private lawsuit by the buyer, and a criminal prosecution by a prosecutor. Different actors, different standards of proof, different clocks. Most of the questions here are really asking which door you are standing in — and the most reliable single question type is what the Administrator can and cannot do without a court.

cells.title: The Administrator — powers and limits
refs: STC 43e Ch. 7 Powers of the State Administrator, p. 143; Injunctions, p. 144

items.x: The Administrator is the state’s senior securities official. Titles vary — Securities Commissioner, Director of the Division of Securities, Secretary of State — and the office is usually a staff rather than a person. The powers and constraints are the same regardless of the label.

The Administrator CAN: make, amend, and rescind rules and forms · issue interpretive and exemptive orders · register and deny, suspend, revoke, cancel, or condition registrations · conduct investigations inside or outside the state · subpoena witnesses and documents · administer oaths and take depositions · examine registrants’ books and records · issue cease-and-desist orders · issue stop orders against securities registrations · impose administrative fines and require restitution · refer matters for criminal prosecution · apply to a court for an injunction or the appointment of a receiver · cooperate with other administrators and with federal regulators.

The Administrator CANNOT: make arrests · prosecute crimes · impose criminal fines or imprisonment · issue an injunction · hold a person in contempt · grant immunity to a witness. Every item on that list is a judicial function requiring a court.

The distinction is worth internalizing as a single sentence: the Administrator is a regulator with subpoena power, not a judge and not a prosecutor. Where the Act needs judicial force, the Administrator goes to court and asks for it.

Rulemaking limits: a rule or order may be adopted only if it is in the public interest and consistent with the purposes of the Act, and no rule may be inconsistent with federal law where federal law preempts. No provision imposing liability applies to an act done in good faith reliance on a rule or order, even if that rule is later amended or held invalid.
“The Administrator issued an injunction against the firm.” Wrong every time — the Administrator issues cease-and-desist orders and asks a court for injunctions.

cells.title: Jurisdiction
refs: STC 43e Ch. 7 Jurisdiction Over Offers, p. 135

items.x: A state’s securities law reaches a transaction if any one of three contacts occurs in that state. Any single one is sufficient, which means a transaction routinely falls under two states’ laws at once.
The three triggers: an offer to SELL or to BUY is made in the state · an offer is ACCEPTED in the state · an acceptance is COMMUNICATED from the state.

An offer is made in a state both where it ORIGINATES and where it is DIRECTED and received. A representative in New York calling a client in California subjects the transaction to both New York and California jurisdiction.

The publication exclusions — an offer is NOT made in a state when it appears in a bona fide newspaper or periodical published OUT of the state; or in one published in the state but with more than TWO-THIRDS of its circulation outside the state in the past twelve months; or in a radio or television program ORIGINATING outside the state.

Internet offers follow the same logic through modern guidance: an offer accessible to residents of a state is generally made there, unless the offer carries an effective legend limiting it and no follow-up is directed into that state.
“Jurisdiction requires the buyer and seller to be in the same state.” Wrong — one contact is enough, and overlapping jurisdiction is normal.
The two-thirds circulation test is a favorite. A magazine published in the state with 70% of its circulation elsewhere falls outside that state’s jurisdiction for the offers it carries.

cells.title: Investigations
refs: STC 43e Ch. 7 Investigations and Subpoenas, p. 143

items.x: The Administrator may investigate whenever it appears necessary to determine whether a person has violated or is about to violate the Act — and may do so inside or outside the state, and may investigate conduct that would violate ANOTHER state’s law, at that state’s request.

Investigative tools: subpoena witnesses to testify · subpoena books, papers, contracts, agreements, and other records · administer oaths and take testimony under oath · take depositions · examine registrants’ records · require written statements under oath.

Procedural protections: a witness may be represented by counsel · a witness may invoke the privilege against self-incrimination · the Administrator cannot grant immunity, so only a court can compel testimony over a valid Fifth Amendment claim · subpoenas are enforced by applying to a court, which may treat non-compliance as contempt.
Investigations may be public or private, and the Administrator may publish information about violations. Nothing requires an investigation to be announced.
“The Administrator granted the witness immunity in exchange for testimony.” Wrong — immunity is judicial.

cells.title: Orders: cease-and-desist, stop, and summary
refs: STC 43e Ch. 2 Denial, Suspension, and Revocation, p. 26; Ch. 7 Cease-and-Desist Orders, p. 144

items.x: A CEASE-AND-DESIST order directs a person to stop conduct that violates the Act. It may issue against ANY person — registered or unregistered, in-state or out-of-state — whose conduct violates the Act and affects the state. Violating a cease-and-desist order is itself a separate violation and may be referred for prosecution.
A STOP ORDER applies to a securities registration, denying, suspending, or revoking its effectiveness. Grounds and procedure are in SEC-8.

A SUMMARY order is one issued without prior notice or hearing, where the Administrator finds immediate action necessary to protect investors or the public interest. It is the exception to the normal due-process sequence, and it carries its own follow-up obligation.

After a summary order the Administrator must promptly notify the affected persons that the order has been entered, state the reasons, and advise that a hearing will be held on written request. On such a request the hearing must be held within FIFTEEN DAYS.
“A summary order may be issued and left in place with no further process.” Wrong — failure to provide the promised hearing can invalidate the order.

cells.title: Administrative action and due process
refs: STC 43e Ch. 7 Administrative Actions Associated with Registration, p. 141; Cancellations and Withdrawals, p. 145

items.x: Before any punitive final action against a registration — denial, suspension, revocation, or the imposition of conditions — three things must happen, and the exam tests the sequence.

The three steps: PRIOR WRITTEN NOTICE stating the grounds and the proposed action · an OPPORTUNITY FOR A HEARING, held within fifteen days of a written request · WRITTEN FINDINGS of fact and conclusions of law.

Two independent requirements must both be satisfied for a punitive action: there must be statutory cause — a ground listed in the Act — AND the action must be in the public interest. Cause alone is not enough, which is why an ancient minor infraction generally does not support revocation.

Non-punitive terminations bypass the machinery because nothing is being alleged. CANCELLATION applies where a registrant no longer exists, has ceased doing business, cannot be located after reasonable search, or is mentally incompetent. WITHDRAWAL is the registrant’s own voluntary exit.

A stem describing mail returned undeliverable, a dissolved entity, or an incapacitated registrant is asking about CANCELLATION, not revocation. A stem describing misconduct is asking about denial, suspension, or revocation.
The Administrator may also impose lesser sanctions — censure, a bar or suspension from association, administrative fines, and restitution — without revoking a registration.

cells.title: Civil liability
refs: STC 43e Ch. 7 Civil Liability for Securities Sold in Violation of the Act, p. 146; Civil Liability for Fraudulent Investment Advice, p. 148

items.x: The Act gives a defrauded or improperly sold BUYER a private right of action against the seller. It is the most powerful remedy in private hands because the buyer need not wait for any regulator to act.

Conduct creating civil liability: selling an unregistered, non-exempt security · selling through an unregistered broker-dealer or agent · selling by means of an untrue statement of material fact or a material omission · selling in violation of a rule or order.

SCIENTER IS NOT REQUIRED. An innocent or merely negligent violation of the registration or sales-conduct rules creates liability. The buyer proves the violation and the purchase; intent is not an element.

RESCISSION formula — the buyer recovers: the price paid, PLUS interest from the date of purchase, PLUS court costs and reasonable attorney fees, MINUS any income received from the security. The buyer must TENDER the security back.
DAMAGES formula — where the buyer has already sold and cannot tender: the same calculation, MINUS the proceeds of that sale. No tender is required.

RESCISSION OFFER — a seller who discovers a violation may make a written offer to unwind the transaction on the same terms a court would order. The BUYER has THIRTY DAYS from receipt to accept. Accepting unwinds the trade and extinguishes liability to that buyer; failing to accept within thirty days waives the buyer’s right of action for that violation.
The thirty days is the buyer’s window to accept. It is not a deadline on the seller to make the offer.

JOINT AND SEVERAL LIABILITY extends beyond the seller to: every person who directly or indirectly controls the seller · every partner, officer, and director of the seller or of a controlling person · every employee who materially aided the sale · every broker-dealer or agent who materially aided it.

The REASONABLE CARE defense: a control person, partner, officer, director, or employee is not liable if they prove they did not know, and in the exercise of reasonable care could not have known, of the facts giving rise to liability. The burden is on the defendant.

STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS — the EARLIER of three years after the violation or two years after discovery. Earlier, not later. A buyer can lose the right to sue three years after the sale even if they discovered the problem yesterday.

A cause of action survives the death of either party. The buyer’s estate may pursue it; a deceased seller’s estate may be pursued. Liability attaches to the transaction, not to the lifespan of the people involved — which is also why a surety bond must remain available for the full limitations period.

Criminal liability requires a WILLFUL violation, and the charge is brought by a prosecutor — the state attorney general or a local prosecutor — not by the Administrator, who may only refer the matter.
Penalties: a fine of up to $5,000, imprisonment for up to 3 years, or both. Multiple violations may be charged separately.
Statute of limitations for criminal prosecution: 5 years after the alleged violation.

What “willful” means here is narrower than intuition suggests. It means the act was DELIBERATE — the person meant to do the thing they did. It does NOT require that they knew the act violated the law. Ignorance of the statute is not a defense.

One narrow defense exists: a person prosecuted for violating a RULE or ORDER may not be imprisoned if they prove they had no actual knowledge of it. The defense covers rules and orders only, never the statutory provisions of the Act itself.
JUDICIAL REVIEW — any final order of the Administrator may be reviewed by a state court. The court reviews on the administrative record; new evidence is generally not admitted.
The petition must be filed within SIXTY DAYS after entry of the final order. Filing does NOT automatically stay the order; a stay must be specifically requested from the court.
Standards of review: findings of FACT are upheld if supported by substantial evidence. Conclusions of LAW are reviewed de novo. Discretionary determinations are reviewed for abuse of discretion.
“Willful means the defendant knew the conduct was illegal.” Wrong — it means the conduct was intentional.

cells.title: SIPC coverage
refs: STC 43e Ch. 3 The Securities Investor Protection Corporation, p. 61

items.x: The investor protection corporation is an industry-funded nonprofit that steps in when a broker-dealer itself fails. It is insolvency protection for customer claims — never a guarantee of investment results.
Coverage: up to $500,000 per customer, of which no more than $250,000 may be cash.
The dollar limits are the setup; the aggregation rules are the question. Coverage is provided per separate customer, meaning per separate ownership capacity or registration.

A cash account and a margin account owned by the same individual at the same firm are ONE customer — combined, one $500,000 limit. An individual account and a joint account with a spouse are TWO customers. An IRA is a separate capacity from an individual taxable account.
In a margin account only the customer’s EQUITY is covered — amounts owed to the firm are subtracted before coverage applies.
A claim exceeding the limits is not extinguished. The customer becomes a general creditor of the broker-dealer for the excess.
Coverage extends to both retail and institutional customers. NOT covered: decline in market value · commodity futures contracts · currency and fixed annuities · unregistered investment contracts.
Representing this coverage as deposit insurance, or as protection against market loss, is itself a misrepresentation and a violation. Link back to COM-3.

SIPC coverage Both Achievable 2.1 and STC p. 61 work the aggregation rules; 2DT gives only the dollar limits. A pattern worth naming rather than leaving implicit. Eleven of the sixteen are gaps in the $2 Textbook, and almost all of those cluster in state registration mechanics — consent to service of process, surety bonds, automatic agent registration, the state net capital rule, the three-business-day custody trigger, the 48-hour brochure rule. That is not a criticism of the source; it is a description of its editorial angle. It teaches the architecture well and the plumbing thinly. STC is the opposite and is where you should go for anything procedural. Achievable sits between them and is usually the best first read when a concept has not landed at all.
